title: Cushioned Burst Multiplex Orchestration - PRD notes
content:
Summary:

This is a working PRD draft exploring a new capacity orchestration approach for Dedicated: "Cushioned Burst Multiplex Orchestration" (CBMO). The core idea is to multiplex short, latency-sensitive microbursts from multiple tenants into a pooled cushion of prewarmed or lightly reserved capacity, with fast admission control and tenant-protection policies so high-fidelity workloads keep tail latency SLOs while the platform smooths cost via time-boxed multiplexing.

Goals and success metrics (MVP):
- Keep 95th/99th token latency within target for latency-first tenants during microbursts (95th < configured SLO).
- Reduce Pro-rata dedicated overprovisioning by 12–25% for bursty tenants across weekly windows.
- No customer-visible preemptions for 'protected' lanes during first 3 months after rollout.
- Provide observability: per-tenant burst-accept rate, cushion-usage, and spillover events in Console.

Problem context / motivation:
- Many Dedicated customers have spiky traffic: short high-concurrency spikes (chat bursts, inference peaks) causing either wasted steady reserve or missed SLOs.
- Current options: customer buys larger steady capacity, relies on on-demand burst credits, or accepts degraded latency when we spill to lower-fidelity variants.
- We need a system that: accepts microbursts quickly, isolates noisy tenants, and decays capacity pressure predictably so operators can reason about cost and safety.

Concept overview (how CBMO works):
1) Cushion layer: an orchestrated pool of warm capacity (mix of warm-vms and preforked containers/VM slices) maintained per-region. The cushion is sized dynamically from historical burst shapes and immediate reservoir signals.
2) Multiplexing admission: short-lived requests can be admitted into the cushion if their predicted tail-latency impact is below a per-pool headroom threshold. Admission uses a fast estimator (see Signals & estimator below).
3) Tenant protection lanes: tenants can opt-in to one of three lanes: PROTECTED (no preemptions, reserved margin), BALANCED (cost-aware, best-effort with controlled throttles), and OPPORTUNISTIC (cheaper, preemptable).
4) Cushion currency and decay: admission consumes cushion credits which decay over a configurable decay window (e.g., 5–15m). Decay smooths transient pressure and prevents long-lasting hammering.
5) Backpressure and fallthrough: when cushion exhausted, traffic follows fallback policies: redirect to dedicated steady capacity, degrade to lower-fidelity model, or apply token-level throttles.

Signals & estimator (fast admission):
- Inputs: current per-tenant inflight RPS, recent per-tenant 99th token latency, model sequence length distribution, cushion occupancy, per-host CPU/GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate estimate.
- Quick estimator: a lightweight quantile mapping learned from serving telemetry (both offline and online). It predicts delta-tail for admitting X extra concurrency. Must be O(1) per decision and resilient to noisy metrics.
- Fallback estimator: conservative rule-based thresholds if telemetry stale.

Isolation controls and safety model:
- Soft fences per-tenant: admission quotas enforce that a tenant cannot consume more than N% of cushion over M minutes without a tenancy escalation.
- Eviction / preemption policy: only OPPORTUNISTIC lane faces immediate preemption; BALANCED tenants can be gently rate-limited first. PROTECTED lane requires an explicit reserve or paid headroom; evictions occur only under catastrophic conditions and produce automatic rollback/notifications.
- Noisy neighbor detection: anomaly detectors mark tenants with >x sigma increase in burst frequency; those tenants are automatically limited and placed into mitigation quarantine (temporary stricter quota).

Billing & product packaging implications:
- Cushion is a managed resource included in Dedicated subscription, but premium "Protected" bandwidth needs an add-on SKU to guarantee headroom margins.
- Metering: cushion consumption is metered as microburst-credits (time-decayed) rather than raw vCPU/GPU-seconds to reflect smoothing. Clear Console docs + token-level cost breakdown required.

Observability / Console surface:
- Real-time cushion dashboard: occupancy, incoming admission rate, fulfillment latency, per-tenant cushion spend, spillover events, per-lane SLO health.
- Alerts: cushion depletion (warn, critical), spike-level anomalies, sudden increase in preemptions.
- Tracing hooks: attach request-level tags when a request was admitted to cushion, preempted, or spilled; helps debugging.

Operational runbook (initial operator flow):
- Normal: monitor cushion occupancy and headroom; if sustained >70% for 15m, trigger autosize suggestion.
- Depletion event: cross-check telemetry, identify top consumers (Console), toggle mitigation quarantine on offenders and escalate to SE if customer impacted.
- Preemption incident: notify affected tenants via Status + per-tenant alerts, engage rollback to increase cushion (emergency spinup) if necessary.

Autoscaling and lifecycle:
- Fast path: cushion scales horizontally using warm prewarmed instances and preforked containers with a short spin-up (30–90s). This supports microburst admission.
- Slow path: if cushion repeatedly saturates, autoscaler recommends a long-living capacity resize for the tenant's steady allocation.
- Stability: to avoid oscillation, scale-downs use exponential decay windows and require low occupant percentage for a sustained cooldown.

Rollout plan (canary -> GA):
1) Internal dogfooding: pick 2 engineering tenants and 1 partner to run as PROTECTED lane with sandboxed cushion. Monitor for 2–4 weeks.
2) Beta: open to selected enterprise customers with billing add-on. Collect metrics and refine admission estimator.
3) GA: expose as default for BALANCED lane; PROTECTED as a paid SKU. Provide migration docs and API flags.

Open design questions / risks:
- Estimator safety: how to maintain estimator accuracy for long-tail sequence distributions? Options: per-model fingerprints vs global estimator.
- Cost accounting complexity: microburst-credits vs direct compute metering — customers will want predictable bills. Need clear conversion and simulations.
- Prewarming cost vs saved reserve: how to calibrate cushion size economically across regions with different queue shapes?
- Legal/Security: does multiplexing cause data residency concerns if cushion spans multi-tenant hardware? Likely require tenancy affinity for PROTECTED lane.

Experiment candidates (short experiments to run):
- A/B cushion sizing: 3 cushion policies (conservative / medium / aggressive) for matched tenant cohorts and measure cost/SLO tradeoffs over 30d windows.
- Admission threshold tuning: expose admission headroom as parameter to a small set of customers and observe tail latency impact.
- Eviction grace policies: compare immediate preemption vs soft ramp-down on recovery time of overall pool.

Implementation notes (engineering checklist):
- Instrument per-request cushion admission tag in tracing and logs.
- Implement lightweight estimator service with offline retraining pipeline (daily) and hot-update hooks.
- Console telemetry: cushion heatmap, per-tenant credit ledger, admission traces.
- API: introduce "burst_lane" enum in Dedicated API with values [PROTECTED, BALANCED, OPPORTUNISTIC] plus "requested_headroom" field for PROTECTED.

Customer-facing copy (draft):
- "Cushioned Burst — Reduce steady dedicated reserve and keep your app responsive during spikes. Choose a protection level that matches SLAs and cost appetite."

Next steps / immediate action items:
- Product: define PROTECTED SKU price bands and headroom SLAs (Priya).
- Eng (serving/runtime): prototype admission estimator and cushion spinup pipeline (Jonah + Ethan).
- SRE: draft initial runbook and SLO alert thresholds (Marta).
- Design: Console mockups for cushion ledger and lane selector (Samira).

Notes to self:
- Keep this draft intentionally rough — we'll convert to formal PRD after experiments and early dogfood results.
- Cross-link with JIRA-DED-5413 (autoscaler telemetry) and CONFLUENCE-PRD-8872 (billing model options).
